chapters.label: A set holds each object once

thumbnail.visual: big text "SETS" in tomato on peach; Xecxec sorting shells into a bucket where duplicates vanish; thin black border and drop shadow.

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Lists allow repeats, and dictionaries need keys. Today we meet the set, a bag of unique values.

scenes.onScreen: "A bag of unique values": three numbered lines (1. A set keeps each value once; 2. Sets have no order and no index; 3.
scenes.animation: & - combine sets like Venn diagrams) and an analogy card: a guest list: each name appears once, and you can quickly ask, is this person on the list?
scenes.narration: A set holds unique values. Duplicates disappear. It has no order, so no index either. Think of a guest list. Each name appears once, and you can quickly ask, is this person on the list? Sets also do maths, like Venn diagrams. A bar gives everything in either set. An ampersand gives what is in both. A minus gives what is in the first but not the second.

scenes.onScreen: sets.py: duplicates vanish; add and test membership
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right; faint indent guide lines
scenes.narration: [HL 1] A set with three items, but pomfret appears twice. [HL 2] The length is two, because the duplicate vanished. [HL 3] Add puts a new item in. [HL 4] Sets have no order, so we use sorted to print them in a stable order. [HL 5] The word in asks, is prawns in the set? True, and sets answer very fast.

code.source:
fish = {"pomfret", "prawns", "pomfret"}
print(len(fish))
fish.add("crab")
print(sorted(fish))
print("prawns" in fish)

scenes.onScreen: The name fish tied to a set of three strings
scenes.animation: Name tags pop in with their arrows to the objects (value and type shown, no addresses); when Python reads a name the arrow glows and the object lights up
scenes.narration: Here is the picture. One name, fish, tied to one set object. Inside are three strings, each one once. The duplicate pomfret never made it in. A set is like a dictionary with only keys, and no values. That is why membership tests are fast, and why the items have no index.

scenes.animation: b, a & b and a - b
scenes.narration: [HL 1] A set of one, two, three. [HL 2] And a set of three, four. [HL 3] The bar is the union. Everything in either set, with no repeats. One, two, three, four. [HL 4] The ampersand is the intersection. Only what is in both. Just three. [HL 5] The minus is the difference. What is in a but not in b. One and two.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the command types with key-tick, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as setops dot py. In the terminal, type python, space, setops dot py. One, two, three, four. Then three. Then one, two.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One: A set keeps each value once and has no order. Two: add puts an item in and in tests membership quickly. Three: | gives everything, & gives what is shared, - gives what is left. Four: Use set for an empty set, because {} is an empty dictionary. Pause the video, and say these ideas out loud, once, slowly.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: curly brackets make a dictionary
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We want an empty set, so we write empty curly brackets. We print the type, and it says dict. Empty curly brackets make an empty dictionary. For an empty set, call the set function with nothing inside. Then the type says set. Only sets with items can use curly brackets.

shorts.title: What is a set?
shorts.hook: "A set is a bag of unique values."
shorts.script: A set is a bag of unique values. Put a value in twice, and only one copy stays. A set has no order, so it has no index either. Think of a guest list. Each name appears once. Make one with curly brackets and commas, or by calling set on a list. It is the quickest way to remove duplicates from your data. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Unique values only.

shorts.title: Fast membership
shorts.hook: "Sets are very fast at one job."
shorts.script: Sets are very fast at one job. Is this value in the set? The word in answers at once, even if the set has a million items. A list has to check each item, one by one. So when you have many values and you keep asking, is it in there, use a set. It is a small change with a big effect. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Fast yes or no.

shorts.title: Set maths
shorts.script: Sets do maths like Venn diagrams. A bar gives the union, everything in either set. An ampersand gives the intersection, only what both sets share. A minus gives the difference, what is in the first set but not the second. With these three, you can answer questions like, who joined both classes, in two short lines. Try it yourself. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.onScreen: A | B · A & B · A - B
shorts.caption: Venn diagrams in code.

shorts.title: Empty set trap
shorts.script: Here is a trap. You write empty equals curly brackets, expecting an empty set. But empty curly brackets make an empty dictionary. Print its type, and it says dict. To make an empty set, call set with nothing inside. Only sets that have items can use curly brackets. Remember this whenever you start with nothing at all. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Use set().

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.hook: "Why did the set refuse to repeat itself?"
shorts.script: Why did the set refuse to repeat itself? It only liked unique experiences. Your challenge. Take the list three, one, three, two, one. Turn it into a set. Print how many unique numbers there are. You should see three. Then print the set itself, using sorted so it appears in order. Share your answer in the comments below. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
